newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parliamentarian arrested for fraud.
newsitem.headline: Japan parliamentarian arrested for fraud.

text.p: Japanese police arrested an opposition lawmaker on Wednesday on suspicion of fraud in connection with his family-run investment society which prosecutors say bilked investors out of millions of yen.
The arrest of Upper House parliamentarian Tatsuo Tomobe follows the arrests on Monday of his wife, son and three other managers of the investment society on suspicion of fraud.
Tomobe and the managers of the society, Orange Kyosai Kumiai, are accused of defrauding depositors of about 145 million yen ($1.18 million) with promises of high interest payments.

The allegations are part of a broader police investigation of the society, which police have said illegally raised more than seven billion yen ($57.3 million) from 2,000 depositors from 1992-96 without any intention of investing the money.
Orange Kyosai went bankrupt last December, ten years after it was established by Tomobe's political support group.

Media reports, based on informal police briefings, have said Tomobe spent one billion yen ($8.1 million) to win his party's endorsement as a candidate for the 1995 Upper House election and may have funnelled money to other opposition politicians.
Tomobe won election in 1995 on the proportional representation list of the largest opposition party Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) after five unsuccessful attempts to win a seat in parliament.
Tomobe, 68, may have used the money to pursuade Shinshinto to overlook his poor polling record and place him high on the party list, media reports quoted investigators as saying.
Officials of Shinshinto, which Tomobe was forced to quit last November when the scandal came to light, scrambled to distance themselves from the disgraced lawmaker and denied allegations of payments.
"We apologise as the party responsible for endorsing him," said Shinshinto General Secretary Takeo Nishioka in a statement.

"Contrary to speculation, no money changed hands. It was absolutely impossible," said Morihiro Hosokawa, a former prime minister, in a written statement. Hosokawa headed the faction of Shinshinto through which Tomobe entered the party.

The embarassment to the self-styled reformist Shinshinto was likely to take pressure off Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, whose one-year tenure has been clouded by bribery scandals at the health and trade ministries.
A political cartoon in the daily Mainichi Shimbun showed Hashimoto looking on gleefully as his archrival, Shinshinto President Ichiro Ozawa, slipped on an orange peel.
"Whether a lawmaker or not, anybody who has committed an evil deed should be punished," Hashimoto told reporters after hearing of the arrest.
The arrest of Tomobe required parliament to take the rare step of lifting the the lawmaker's immunity from arrest while the legislature is in session.
Under Japanese law, a lawmaker cannot be arrested while parliament is in session unless the arrest is approved in advance by parliament or the lawmaker is caught committing an illegal act.
In December 1995, former labour minister Toshio Yamaguchi was arrested in connection with a loan scandal involving two failed credit unions. ($=122 yen)
